# R Workshop 2


## How to read this document

Every grey box below is a *code chunk*: R code that actually runs when this
document is knitted. The white box underneath it is the *output* that R
produced. The text around them tells you what the code does, why it is written
that way, and how to read the output.

Three habits will serve you for the whole workshop:

1. Run a chunk, then look at the output before moving on. R is an interactive
   language. Guessing what a line did is slower than checking.
2. When a line is unfamiliar, take it apart from the inside out. `mean(x)` is a
   *function* called `mean` applied to an *argument* `x`.
3. If something breaks, read the error message from the bottom up. R usually
   names the function that failed.

Some vocabulary that the rest of the document assumes:

- An **object** is a named thing stored in memory. `x <- 5` creates an object
  called `x`. The `<-` is the *assignment* operator; `=` also works in most
  places, but R programmers use `<-` for assignment by convention.
- A **function** is a named piece of code that takes inputs and returns an
  output. `sqrt(16)` returns `4`.
- An **argument** is one of those inputs. Arguments can be given by position
  (`round(3.14159, 2)`) or by name (`round(3.14159, digits = 2)`). Naming them
  is slower to type and much easier to read six months later.
- A **package** is a bundle of functions written by somebody else. You install
  it once, then load it in every session where you want it.

The Workshop 1 material was about the language itself: how R stores values, how
loops and conditions work, and how to lay out a script so another person can
read it. That material is base R, meaning it ships with R and needs no packages.

Sections 3 and 4 are different in kind. `dplyr` and `ggplot2` are packages. They
do not add anything R could not already do; they add a consistent vocabulary for
doing it. In base R, keeping the rows of a data frame `df` where column `Food`
exceeds 100 looks like `df[df$Food > 100, ]`. In `dplyr` it is
`filter(df, Food > 100)`. The second is a few characters longer and far easier
to read, and once you know the pattern it transfers to every other verb in the
package.



## 3. Introduction to Data Cleaning: Dplyr and the Tidyverse

### 3.1 What is the Tidyverse?

R ships with a few thousand functions. Everything else lives in packages that
other people wrote and published. A package has to be *installed* once per
machine (it downloads files onto your hard drive) and *loaded* once per R
session (it makes its functions visible to your code).

`install.packages("dplyr")` installs. `library(dplyr)` loads. Running
`library()` on a package you never installed is an error; running
`install.packages()` every time you knit is slow and rude to the mirror server.
`pacman::p_load()` folds the two into one call: it checks whether each package
is already installed, installs the missing ones, then loads all of them.

The `::` in `pacman::p_load` means "the `p_load` function from the `pacman`
package". Writing it that way lets you call a function without loading the whole
package, and it makes the source of the function obvious to a reader.

```{r}
# p_load() installs a package only if it is missing, then loads it.
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, here, skimr)

```

Three things arrived in that one line:

- `tidyverse` is a *meta-package*. Loading it loads `dplyr` (data manipulation),
  `ggplot2` (plots), `readr` (reading files), `tibble` (a modern data frame),
  `tidyr` (reshaping), `stringr` (text), `forcats` (factors) and `purrr`
  (iteration). The startup message lists them, and it also lists *conflicts*:
  `dplyr::filter()` masks `stats::filter()`, so from here on a plain `filter()`
  means the `dplyr` one.
- `here` builds file paths that work no matter which sub-folder you are sitting
  in. Section 3.2 uses it.
- `skimr` produces a compact summary of a whole data frame.

The "Tidyverse" is a collection of R packages designed to work together seamlessly and follow a consistent set of principles for data manipulation and analysis. It provides a cohesive and powerful toolkit for data cleaning, transformation, visualization, and modeling, and is the "industry standard" for many data operations in R.

`Dplyr` is one of the core packages within the Tidyverse. It offers a simple, consistent approach to doing all your basic data tidying operations.

The shared principle worth naming now is **tidy data**. A table is tidy when

1. each row is one observation,
2. each column is one variable,
3. each cell is one value.

Our CPI file is not tidy when it arrives: the years run across the top as column
headers, so a single row mixes 23 different observations. Section 3.2 fixes
that, and the fix is most of the reason that import chunk is so long.

### 3.2 5+1 functions

The "80/20" rule applies in many contexts; that 80% of effects come from 20% of causes.

Example: 80% of my productivity comes from 20% of my working time!

In Dplyr, there's a similar dynamic with the following functions, perhaps even more extreme: 90% of your data cleaning can be covered by the following 5+1 functions:

-   `select()`
-   `mutate()`
-   `filter()`
-   `arrange()`
-   `summarise()`

and,

-   `group_by()`

The first five do various operations, such as subsetting and altering your data. `group_by()` is separated, because while it's almost never used alone, it augments the other functions and adds a whole new dimension of use.

All six share one contract. Learning it once saves you from six separate sets of
rules:

- The **first argument is always a data frame**. That is what makes them
  chainable with the pipe in Section 3.6.
- Later arguments refer to **column names without quotes**. Inside
  `filter(food_cpi, Food > 100)`, the bare word `Food` means "the column called
  Food in `food_cpi`". Outside the function, typing `Food` on its own is an
  error, because no object of that name exists in your workspace. This behavior
  is called *data masking*, and it is the most common source of confusion for
  people arriving from Python.
- They **return a new data frame and never modify the one you passed in**. That
  is worth demonstrating rather than asserting, which we do as soon as the data
  is loaded.

Before we get to the commands themselves, we need to import our data. I'll set this up in one cell; a few of these commands will be seen again later.


The next chunk re-loads four packages that `tidyverse` already loaded above. It
is redundant, and it is harmless: loading a package a second time does nothing.
It is kept because it documents which package each function in the import chunk
comes from - `read_csv` from `readr`, `here` from `here`, `mutate` and `rename`
from `dplyr`, `as_tibble` from `tibble`.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
```

The import chunk transposes the raw file. Transposing means flipping rows and
columns, and it is easier to see on a table small enough to print whole:

```{r}
# A toy table in the same shape as the raw CPI file: one row per product group,
# one column per year. Backticks are needed around names that start with a
# digit, because 2000 on its own is a number, not a name.
transpose_demo <- tibble(
  group  = c("A", "B"),
  `2000` = c(1, 2),
  `2001` = c(3, 4)
)

transpose_demo

# t() is base R's transpose. Rows become columns, columns become rows.
t(transpose_demo)
```

Two things to notice in the transposed output. First, the year labels `2000` and
`2001` are no longer column names; they have become *row names*, printed down
the left edge. Second, every value is now in quotation marks. `t()` returns a
**matrix**, and a matrix holds exactly one type of value throughout. Mixing the
text `"A"` with the number `1` forces the whole thing to text. Both facts drive
the code in the import chunk: it has to recover the years from the row names,
and it has to convert the numbers back from text.

Two lines in the import chunk use `%>%`, the pipe. Section 3.6 covers it
properly. For now, read `x %>% f(y)` as `f(x, y)`: the thing on the left becomes
the first argument of the function on the right. So
`cpi_t %>% mutate(Year = year_col)` is the same call as
`mutate(cpi_t, Year = year_col)`.

Now the real import. Read it once top to bottom, then read the commentary that
follows it.

```{r}
# The shared data folder sits at the top level of the repository. here() anchors
# on the R project file, so build the path from there. The fallback covers the
# case where the project is opened at the repository root instead of at r/.
data_dir <- here("..", "data")
if (!dir.exists(data_dir)) data_dir <- here("data")

# read csv file in as data
cpi <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "food_cpi.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# transpose
cpi_t <- t(cpi)

# assign first row as column names
colnames(cpi_t) <- as.character(cpi_t[1, ])

# remove first row from dataframe
cpi_t <- cpi_t[-1, ]

# get index as year column
year_col <- row.names(cpi_t)

# turn cpi_t to tibble datatype
cpi_t <- as_tibble(cpi_t)

# replace years
cpi_t <- cpi_t %>%
  mutate(Year = year_col)

# rename columns
cpi_t <- rename(cpi_t, "Energy" = "Energy 7", "Food" = "Food 5", "Goods" = "Goods 8", "Shelter" = "Shelter 6", "Services" = "Services 9", 
                "All_items" = "All-items",
                "Household_operations_furniture_equipment" = "Household operations, furnishings and equipment",
                "All_items_but_food_energy" = "All-items excluding food and energy 7",
                "All_items_excluding_energy" = "All-items excluding energy 7",
                "Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis" = "Alcoholic beverages, tobacco products and recreational cannabis",
                "Recreation_education_books" = "Recreation, education and reading",
                "Clothing_and_footwear" = "Clothing and footwear",
                "Health_personal_care" = "Health and personal care")

colnames(cpi_t)

cpi_t <- cpi_t %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

cpi_t
```

#### Walking through the import

**The path.** `here()` builds an absolute file path starting from the root of
your project. It finds that root by walking up from the current folder until it
sees a marker file. In this repository the marker is `r/r.Rproj`, so `here()`
resolves to the `r` folder, and `here("..", "data")` resolves to the `data`
folder next to it at the repository top level. The `".."` means "go up one
level", exactly as in a file explorer.

The `if (!dir.exists(data_dir))` line is a guard. `dir.exists()` returns `TRUE`
or `FALSE`, and `!` flips it. The sentence reads: if that folder is *not* there,
use `here("data")` instead, which is the right answer when somebody opens the
project at the repository root rather than at `r/`. Path problems are the most
common reason a classmate's notebook fails to run on your machine. Never write
`read_csv("C:/Users/yourname/Desktop/food_cpi.csv")`. That path exists on
exactly one computer in the world.

`file.path()` glues folder and file names together with the right separator for
your operating system, which is why it beats pasting a `"/"` in yourself.

**Reading.** `read_csv()` is `readr`'s CSV reader. It returns a **tibble**: a
data frame with better printing and no surprise type conversions. The
`show_col_types = FALSE` argument suppresses the block of text that otherwise
reports every column's guessed type. We suppress it only because the data gets
restructured immediately.

**Transposing.** `t(cpi)` gives a character matrix, exactly as in the toy
example. Here is the raw file's shape before the flip:

```{r}
# First four columns of the raw import: product groups down the side, years
# across the top. This is the untidy layout described in Section 3.1.
cpi[, 1:4]
```

Each row is a product group and each column is a year, so one row holds 23
separate observations. After `t()`, each row is a year and each column is a
product group, which is what we want.

**Recovering the header.** `cpi_t[1, ]` is the first row of the matrix, which
after transposing holds the product-group names. Square brackets are R's
subsetting operator, and inside them the order is always `[rows, columns]`;
leaving one side blank means "all of them". `colnames(cpi_t) <- ...` writes
those names onto the matrix, and `cpi_t <- cpi_t[-1, ]` then deletes that row. A
negative index in R means "everything except this", not "count from the end" as
it does in Python.

**Recovering the years.** `row.names(cpi_t)` pulls the row labels, which are the
year strings, into a character **vector** called `year_col`. A vector is R's
most basic data structure: an ordered sequence of values that all share one
type. A data frame is, underneath, a list of equal-length vectors.

**Back to a tibble.** `as_tibble()` converts the matrix into a tibble. Row names
are dropped in the process, which is why `year_col` had to be saved first, and
why the next line puts it back as a real column using `mutate()`.

**Renaming.** The Statistics Canada column names carry footnote markers
(`"Food 5"`, `"Energy 7"`) plus spaces and commas. Names like that have to be
wrapped in backticks every time you use them. `rename()` takes pairs in the form
`new_name = "old_name"` and returns a tibble with the names swapped. The bare
`colnames(cpi_t)` line then prints the result so you can check the rename worked
before going further.

**Fixing the types.** Everything is still text at this point, a side effect of
`t()`. `mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))` fixes it. `across()` applies
one function to many columns, `everything()` selects all of them, and
`as.numeric` converts text to numbers. Note that `as.numeric` is passed *without*
parentheses: we are handing `across()` the function itself, not the result of
calling it.

Reading the printed tibble at the bottom: the header line says
`# A tibble: 23 x 16`, meaning 23 rows and 16 columns. Under each column name is
its type, `<dbl>` for double-precision numbers. Tibbles print only the first ten
rows by default, and the footer names the columns that did not fit on screen.

#### The verbs do not modify your data

This is the point most easily missed, and missing it costs people hours later.

```{r}
# select() returns a NEW tibble with two columns...
select(cpi_t, Year, Food)

# ...but cpi_t itself is untouched: still 16 columns.
ncol(cpi_t)
```

The result of `select()` was printed and then thrown away, because it was never
assigned to anything. `cpi_t` still has all 16 columns. To keep a result you
must assign it: `small <- select(cpi_t, Year, Food)`. Coming from Python, the
trap is expecting something like an in-place method. There is none here.

`glimpse()` is a compact structural summary: one line per column, showing the
name, the type, and the first few values. Use it when a data frame is too wide
to print.

```{r}
dplyr::glimpse(cpi_t)
```

Read it as a rotated preview. `$ Year <dbl> 2000, 2001, 2002, ...` says there is
a column named `Year`, it holds doubles, and it starts at 2000. Sixteen lines of
output means sixteen columns.

`class()` and `typeof()` both describe a column, but they answer different
questions. `typeof()` reports how R stores the value in memory: `"double"`,
`"integer"`, `"character"`, `"logical"`, `"list"`. `class()` reports how R
should *treat* it: `"numeric"`, `"character"`, `"factor"`, `"Date"`. They often
agree, and when they disagree the difference is informative. A date has class
`"Date"` and type `"double"`, because R stores dates as a count of days since
1970-01-01.

`sapply(df, f)` applies the function `f` to every column of `df` and returns the
answers as a named vector. It is base R's version of the `across()` idea.

```{r}
# Class (factor, character, numeric, Date, etc.)
sapply(cpi_t, class)

# Low-level storage type (integer, double, logical, character, list)
sapply(cpi_t, typeof)

```

Every column reports class `numeric` and type `double`, which confirms the
`as.numeric` conversion reached all 16 columns. Had any column been left as
`"character"`, arithmetic on it would fail later with the error "non-numeric
argument to binary operator".

One class you will meet constantly, and that is absent here: a **factor** is R's
type for a categorical variable with a fixed set of allowed values, called its
*levels*. Underneath, a factor is stored as integer codes plus a lookup table of
labels, which is why `class()` says `"factor"` while `typeof()` says
`"integer"`. Factors matter because `ggplot2` uses level order to decide the
order of bars and legend entries, and because regression functions turn factors
into dummy variables automatically. We build one in Section 3.6.

`skim()` from `skimr` is a fuller report: how many rows and columns, how many
missing values per column, and the mean, standard deviation, quantiles and a
small text histogram for every numeric column.

```{r}
# skimr was loaded in the first chunk of this notebook.
skimr::skim(cpi_t)

```

Read `n_missing` first (zero everywhere here, so nothing is missing yet) and
`complete_rate` next (1.00, the same fact as a proportion). After that, `p0` and
`p100` are the minimum and maximum and `p50` is the median. Compare `Gasoline`
with `Clothing_and_footwear`: gasoline runs from about 100 to 247 across the
sample while clothing barely moves and spends most of the period below its 2002
base of 100. That spread is why economists rarely quote a single inflation
number without saying which basket it refers to.

### 3.3 `select()`

`select()` is conceptually the simplest, and a good place to start for our data cleaning. It is also probably the simplest: you pass in a dataframe, and name the columns you want to keep. It returns just those columns.

As you can see, `cpi_t` has a lot of non-food columns. We don't want those. We'll select just `"Year"`, `"Food"`, and `"All_items_but_food_energy"` (the names we assigned in the import chunk above), leaving out the others, calling this `food_cpi`

The generic R function `colnames()` is useful here, in case we need to alter our selection.

Column names can be given bare (`Year`) or quoted (`"Year"`). Both work in
`select()`. Bare names are the tidyverse convention; quotes are needed only when
a name contains spaces or starts with a digit, and even then backticks are the
usual choice. The code below uses quotes, which is perfectly valid and slightly
more defensive.

```{r}
colnames(cpi_t)
```

```{r}
food_cpi <- select(cpi_t, "Year", "Food", "All_items_but_food_energy")

food_cpi
```

The result is a new tibble with 23 rows and 3 columns, assigned to `food_cpi`.
Column order in the output follows the order you named them, not the order they
had in `cpi_t`, so `select()` doubles as a reordering tool.

#### Exercise (`select()`)

Create new dataframes as I did above, each including the `"Year"` column and a selection of others:


-   `consumables_cpi`, including any goods which are consumed quickly (like food, energy, etc)
-   `durables_cpi`, including any goods which *aren't* consumed quickly (like clothing, transport, etc)
-   `services_cpi`, including any items which are primarily services performed by a person

These three tibbles are used again later, `durables_cpi` and `services_cpi` in
Exercises 2 and 3 of Section 4.2, so run this chunk even if you would have
grouped the categories differently. The `library(dplyr)` call at the top is
another harmless repeat.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

#colnames(cpi_t)

consumables_cpi <- select(cpi_t, "Year", "Gasoline", "Energy", "Food", "Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis")

consumables_cpi

durables_cpi <- select(cpi_t, "Year", "Household_operations_furniture_equipment", "Clothing_and_footwear", "Shelter", "Transportation", "Recreation_education_books")

durables_cpi

services_cpi <- select(cpi_t, "Year", "Health_personal_care", "Services")
services_cpi

```

Three chunks of output, one per tibble, because a bare object name on its own
line prints that object. Note that the classification is a judgment call, not a
fact: `Shelter` is grouped with durables here, but rent is arguably a service.
Say what you did and why, and be consistent.

Now try something new. If you call `everything()` inside of a `select()` statement, it'll return all columns specified up to that point, then all remaining columns after it.

Move `Year` to the left of the dataset by using `select()` with `Year` and `everything()`

```{r}
# answer
select(cpi_t, Year, everything())
```

`Year` is now the first column and the other 15 follow in their original order.
`everything()` is one of the *tidyselect helpers*, a small family of functions
that pick columns by pattern instead of by name. The others you will use most:

```{r}
# starts_with(): every column whose name begins with this text
names(select(cpi_t, starts_with("All")))

# contains(): every column whose name contains this text anywhere.
# Matching is case-insensitive by default, so "energy" also finds "Energy".
names(select(cpi_t, contains("energy")))

# a leading minus sign drops columns instead of keeping them
names(select(cpi_t, -Gasoline, -Energy))
```

Use explicit names when the selection is short and stable, and helpers when the
selection is long or when new columns with the same naming pattern might arrive
later. `names()` and `colnames()` return the same thing for a data frame; the
calls above are wrapped in `names()` only to keep the printed output short.

```{r}
cpi_t
```

Now move all non-compound CPI types to the left: `"Food"`, `"Shelter"`, `"Transportation"`, `"Gasoline"`, `"Energy"`, `"Goods"`, and `"Services"`.

```{r}
# answer




```

Select just the `"Food"` column. Does it become a vector, or stay as a tibble?

```{r}
select(cpi_t, Food)


```

The header says `# A tibble: 23 x 1`, so the answer is that it stays a tibble.
`select()` always returns a data frame, even a one-column one. That consistency
is deliberate: it means the next verb in a chain always receives what it
expects. When you actually want the bare numbers, use `pull()` or `$`:

```{r}
class(select(cpi_t, Food))  # tibble
class(pull(cpi_t, Food))    # numeric vector
class(cpi_t$Food)           # numeric vector, base R version of pull()
```

Reach for `pull()` or `$` when you need to feed a single column to something
that wants a vector, such as `mean()` or `plot()`.

```{r}
cpi_t
```


### 3.4 `mutate()`

The `mutate()` function is a tool for performing calculations or transformations on data within a dataframe. You can create new columns based on existing data or modify existing columns, enabling you to process your data for further analysis.

Our datasets contain the Consumer Price Indices for various types of goods. To transform these into inflation percentages, we'll need to subtract the previous year's value, then divide by it.

The `lag()` function is used with a data column: you input this column, and it moves each entry "down" one row. Our data goes from 2000 onwards, so the 2000 value is moved to 2001, 2001 to 2002, etc. The first year doesn't have a prior value, so this is filled with an `NA`.

`NA` is R's marker for a missing value. It is not zero and not an empty string.
Any arithmetic involving `NA` returns `NA`, which is the correct and honest
answer: if you do not know last year's price, you cannot know this year's growth
rate.

Before the calculation, look at what `lag()` actually does. The chunk below
builds a two-column comparison and plots both series.

```{r}
# select() keeps Year and Food; mutate() adds the shifted copy next to it.
lag_demo <- food_cpi %>%
  select(Year, Food) %>%
  mutate(Food_lagged = lag(Food))

# head() prints the first n rows. The 2000 row shows the NA that lag() creates.
head(lag_demo, 4)
```

Row by row: in 2001 the `Food` column holds 97.4 and `Food_lagged` holds 93.3,
which is 2000's value. `lag()` has not changed any number; it has moved the
whole column down by one row and filled the gap at the top with `NA`.

```{r}
# pivot_longer() stacks the two columns into one, adding a "series" column that
# records which one each value came from. ggplot2 wants data in this long shape
# when you plot several series with one geom.
lag_demo_long <- lag_demo %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(Food, Food_lagged),  # which columns to stack
    names_to  = "series",              # new column holding the old column names
    values_to = "index_value"          # new column holding the values
  )

ggplot(lag_demo_long, aes(x = Year, y = index_value, color = series)) +
  geom_line(na.rm = TRUE) +            # na.rm = TRUE: drop the 2000 NA quietly
  geom_point(size = 1.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 0: What lag() does to a column",
    x     = "Year",
    y     = "Food CPI (2002 = 100)",
    color = "Series"
  )
```

The two lines have identical shape; the lagged one is the same curve shifted one
year to the right, and it starts in 2001 rather than 2000 because its first
value is `NA`. The vertical distance between the two lines at any year is
exactly `food_change` for that year, which is what the next chunk computes.

```{r}
food_cpi_mutate <- mutate(food_cpi, 
                          # create change of Food CPI versus lagged period's CPI: difference since last year
                          food_change = Food - lag(Food), 
                          
                          # create percentage Food CPI change: subtract previous CPI then divide by it
                          food_change_percent = 100*(food_change)/lag(Food),
                          
                          
                          # then do change and change percent values for All_items_but_food_energy variable
                          All_items_change = All_items_but_food_energy - lag(All_items_but_food_energy),
                          All_items_change_percent = 100*(All_items_change)/lag(All_items_but_food_energy))

food_cpi_mutate
```

The percentage formula deserves a slow reading, because the brackets are doing
real work.

`food_change_percent = 100 * (food_change) / lag(Food)`

- `food_change` was created two lines earlier, in the same `mutate()` call. That
  is allowed and useful: `mutate()` evaluates its arguments in order, so a new
  column can be used by any column defined after it. Written out, `food_change`
  is `Food - lag(Food)`, this year's index minus last year's.
- Dividing by `lag(Food)` makes it a proportion *of last year's level*. The
  denominator is last year, not this year. Using `Food` as the denominator would
  be a different and less standard quantity.
- Multiplying by 100 turns the proportion into percent. The whole expression is
  read left to right for multiply and divide, so `100 * (food_change) / lag(Food)`
  computes `(100 * food_change) / lag(Food)`, which is the same number as
  `100 * (food_change / lag(Food))`.

Where students go wrong is dropping the brackets around the numerator. Writing
`100 * Food - lag(Food) / lag(Food)` is valid R and completely wrong: `/` binds
tighter than `-`, so R computes `(100 * Food) - (lag(Food) / lag(Food))`, which
is 100 times the price index minus 1. Check the magnitude of your first result.
An inflation rate of 9000 percent means you lost a bracket.

Reading the output: 2022 shows `food_change` of 14.0 index points and
`food_change_percent` of 8.89 percent, against an `All_items_change_percent` of
4.96 percent. That single row drives most of the visual argument in Section 4.

As you can see, `mutate()` creates new variable columns. You specify a new column name, like we did with `food_change`, and make it equal to a number, value, or calculation. This can include arithmetic operations, like addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (\*) and division (/). You can also take exponents, and do a whole range of other operations for other data types.

Sticking to just numeric data as we are, the arithmetic operations give us a solid base to work with.

One more property worth stating plainly: these operations are *vectorized*.
`Food - lag(Food)` is not a loop over 23 rows that you have to write; R applies
the subtraction element by element across both vectors at once and returns a
vector of 23 answers. Almost every arithmetic operation in R behaves this way,
and code that uses it is both shorter and faster than the equivalent `for` loop.

##### Note:

The variables we created involving a `lag()` all start with a `NA` value - for the first period of observation, we don't have a prior period's value to pull! As a result, it fetches a `NA`, and we don't get `_change` or `_change_percent` values for the first row.

In some analyses, you'd drop the first row to have a consistent dataset with full coverage. Since we're still interested in 2000's CPI values, we're going to leave it. However, when we do operations involving these columns, we'll have to use a special method to tell R to ignore these values.

We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

```{r}
# How many missing values did the lag introduce? One per lagged column.
sum(is.na(food_cpi_mutate$food_change))

# And what a summary statistic does about it if you say nothing:
mean(food_cpi_mutate$food_change)
```

`is.na(x)` returns `TRUE`/`FALSE` for each element, and `sum()` counts the
`TRUE`s because `TRUE` counts as 1. One missing value, as expected. The `mean()`
call returns `NA`, not an error and not a number: R refuses to guess. Section
3.7 shows the fix.

#### Exercise (`mutate()`)

Working with `consumables_cpi`, calculate the yearly change in `Gasoline`, `Energy`, and `Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis` CPI values, and then the percentage changes, as we did above with `food_cpi`

```{r}
# Every new column is defined inside the mutate() call, so the column names on
# the right-hand side are looked up in consumables_cpi.
# Note the bracketing: the numerator must be wrapped before dividing by the lag,
# and the multiplier for a percentage is 100, not 0.1.

consumables_cpi_mutate <- mutate(
  consumables_cpi,

  gasoline_change = Gasoline - lag(Gasoline),
  gasoline_change_percent = 100 * (Gasoline - lag(Gasoline)) / lag(Gasoline),

  a_t_c_change = Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis - lag(Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis),
  a_t_c_change_percent = 100 * (Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis - lag(Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis)) / lag(Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis),

  energy_change = Energy - lag(Energy),
  energy_change_percent = 100 * (Energy - lag(Energy)) / lag(Energy)
)

consumables_cpi_mutate


```

This version writes `Gasoline - lag(Gasoline)` out again in the percentage line
rather than reusing `gasoline_change`. Both styles work. Reusing the earlier
column is shorter and keeps the two definitions in sync if you edit one;
repeating the expression makes each line readable on its own. Pick one and stay
with it inside a single project.

Gasoline is the series to look at here. Its percentage change runs from minus
17.5 percent in 2009 to plus 31.2 percent in 2021, and it changes sign seven
times over 22 years. Food never moved more than 8.9 percent in a year and never
fell at all. Energy prices are volatile in a way food prices are not, which is
part of why Statistics Canada publishes an "excluding food and energy" series in
the first place.

You can use the `transmute()` function to create new variables, and keep only these. Create a new dataframe, `real_cpis` using transmute. Create the following real price indices:
- `real_food` equal to `Food` divided by `All_items`
- `real_gas` equal to `Gasoline` divided by `All_items`
- `real_shelter` equal to `Shelter` divided by `All_items`
- `real_energy` equal to `Energy` divided by `All_items`

Also include the `Year` column!

```{r}

real_cpis<-transmute(cpi_t, Year,
                     real_food = Food / All_items,
                     real_gas = Gasoline / All_items,
                     real_shelter = Shelter / All_items,
                     real_energy = Energy/ All_items)

real_cpis




```

`transmute()` is `mutate()` plus a `select()` of only the new columns. `Year`
appears in the output because it is listed as a bare column name inside the
call; without it, the years would be gone.

Economically, dividing a component index by the all-items index gives a *relative
price*: the price of that good measured in units of the average consumption
basket. Both series share the same 2002 base of 100, so every ratio equals
exactly 1 in 2002, and a value above 1 means that good has grown more expensive
than the basket since then. `real_food` sits at or just below 1 through 2006, exactly 1 in the 2002 base
year, crosses
above it in 2007, and reaches 1.13 by 2022, so food has outpaced general
inflation over the sample without doing so every single year. `real_gas` is far
more erratic: 1.44 in 2008, back to 1.07 in 2020, then 1.64 in 2022. Relative
prices are not trends; they move whenever one component moves faster than the
basket, in either direction.

A note on the function itself: `transmute()` has been superseded in current
`dplyr`, meaning it still works and is not going away, but the documentation now
points to `mutate(.keep = "none")` instead. Both produce the same result here.


### 3.5 `filter()`

The filter() function in dplyr lets you extract subsets of data based on specific conditions, allowing you to easily filter rows from a dataframe based on your requirements.

You feed in a dataframe, and a condition to apply to one or more columns. It returns only the rows which meet said requirement. Hence, it's a `filter()`.

`select()` has a similar effect, just focused on columns. However, most datasets will have more (sometimes many, many more) rows than columns; naming them individually will rapidly become impractical. Instead, we'll create "boolean conditions", logical statements returning `TRUE` or `FALSE`. `filter()` will keep only rows for which this value comes up as `TRUE`.

The comparison operators that produce those conditions:

| Operator | Meaning                  |
|----------|--------------------------|
| `>`      | greater than             |
| `>=`     | greater than or equal to |
| `<`      | less than                |
| `<=`     | less than or equal to    |
| `==`     | equal to                 |
| `!=`     | not equal to             |

The one that catches everybody is `==`. A single `=` is assignment, not
comparison. `filter(df, Year = 2020)` is an error; `filter(df, Year == 2020)` is
the test you meant.

```{r}
food_cpi_mutate
```

```{r}

filter(food_cpi_mutate, Food>100.0)

```

20 of the 23 rows survive. `Food > 100` is evaluated once per row, producing a
vector of 23 `TRUE`/`FALSE` values, and `filter()` keeps the rows where the
answer is `TRUE`. The three dropped years are 2000, 2001 and 2002, the years
before and at the 2002 base of the index.

```{r}
#compare Food col values which are less than the value of all_items....

filter(food_cpi_mutate, Food<All_items_but_food_energy)


```

Three rows: 2000, 2003 and 2004. A condition does not have to compare a column
to a constant. Here both sides are columns, so the comparison is made row by
row. These are the only years in which the food index sat below the
food-and-energy-excluded index, and after 2004 food never falls back below it.

```{r}
food_cpi_mutate$food_change
```

`$` extracts one column as a plain vector, which is why this prints as a run of
numbers rather than a table. The leading `NA` is the 2000 value, and this is a
useful habit: when a filter behaves strangely, print the raw column and look for
`NA`s.

Let's get just the years with a really high increase in food prices, like 4% or more.

```{r}

high_inflation <- filter(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent > 4.0)
high_inflation

```

Three years clear the 4 percent bar: 2001, 2009 and 2022. Note what happened to
the 2000 row. Its `food_change_percent` is `NA`, so the condition evaluates to
`NA` rather than `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and `filter()` drops any row whose condition
is not definitely `TRUE`. That is a deliberate design choice and a common source
of quietly shrinking data frames. If you want to keep the missing rows, say so
explicitly with `filter(df, is.na(x) | x > 4)`.

As you can see, `filter()` works by us passing in a dataframe (`food_cpi_mutate`), and then naming a column (`food_change_percent`) as part of a boolean condition. In our case, `food_change_percent > 4.0` returns TRUE for all rows where we have a greater than 4% inflation in food prices; `filter()` then creates a dataframe with just these values in it.

Filtering is easier to trust when you can see which rows went and which stayed.
The chunk below labels every row with its fate and then plots all of them.

```{r}
# case_when() checks conditions in order and returns the value after the ~ for
# the first one that matches. The order matters: the is.na() test has to come
# first, because NA > 4 is NA rather than FALSE and would fall through.
filter_demo <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  mutate(status = case_when(
    is.na(food_change_percent)  ~ "no value (NA)",
    food_change_percent > 4     ~ "kept by filter()",
    TRUE                        ~ "dropped by filter()"
  ))

ggplot(filter_demo, aes(x = Year, y = food_change_percent, fill = status)) +
  # geom_col() draws one bar per row, with height equal to y.
  geom_col(na.rm = TRUE) +
  # The dashed line is the threshold used in the filter() call above.
  geom_hline(yintercept = 4, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 0b: Which rows survive filter(food_change_percent > 4)",
    x     = "Year",
    y     = "Food CPI change (percent)",
    fill  = "Row status"
  )
```

Three bars cross the dashed line at 4 percent, and those are exactly the three
rows `filter()` returned: 2001, 2009 and 2022. Every bar below the line was
dropped. The year 2000 has no bar at all, because its value is `NA` and
`na.rm = TRUE` told `geom_col()` to leave it out rather than warn about it. That
missing bar is the visual form of the rule stated above: a row with `NA` in the
filtered column is dropped, not kept.

#### Exercise (`filter()`)

```{r}
food_cpi_mutate
```

```{r}
# create a DataFrame from `food_cpi_mutate` with just the rows where Food is greater than 100.0


```

```{r}
# create a DataFrame from `food_cpi_mutate` with just the rows where Food is greater than All_items_but_food_energy


```

```{r}
# create a DataFrame from `food_cpi_mutate` with just the rows where food_change is less than All_items_change



# now create a DataFrame from `food_cpi_mutate` with just the rows where food_change is greater than 1


# now create a DataFrame where food_change is less than All_items change, AND food_change is greater than 1

# hint! you can input multiple conditions separated by commas


```

Now you've learned how to filter with multiple conditions. By default, `filter(df, condition_1, condition_2)` returns rows where *all* conditions are met. So, the conditions all have to evaluate to TRUE.

You can also join conditions with `|`, meaning *OR*. As long as one of these evaluates as TRUE, the overall statement will evaluate as TRUE, and you'll return the row.

The three logical operators, and what they do to a pair of `TRUE`/`FALSE`
values:

| Expression | Result |
|------------|--------|
| `TRUE & TRUE` | `TRUE` |
| `TRUE & FALSE` | `FALSE` |
| `TRUE \| FALSE` | `TRUE` |
| `FALSE \| FALSE` | `FALSE` |
| `!TRUE` | `FALSE` |

`&` is AND, `|` is OR, `!` is NOT. AND makes a filter stricter and returns fewer
rows; OR makes it looser and returns more.

```{r}
food_cpi_mutate
```

```{r}
# create the last dataframe again, but using an explicit & symbol between conditions rather than a comma

# hint! Wrap each condition in brackets () to make it easier to read and check


filter(food_cpi_mutate, (food_change < All_items_change) & (food_change > 1))



# create a dataframe with the same conditions stated, but joined with | instead

filter(food_cpi_mutate, (food_change < All_items_change) | (food_change > 1))


```

The contrast is the whole lesson. The `&` version returns 3 rows: 2002, 2003 and
2016, the only years where food rose more than one index point *and* still rose
by less than the all-items series. The `|` version returns 22 rows, everything
except 2000, because almost every year satisfies at least one of the two
conditions and 2000 satisfies neither (both of its inputs are `NA`).

The brackets around each condition are not required by R, which already gives
`<` and `>` higher precedence than `&`. They are there because a reader should
not have to remember the precedence table to check your work.

You *can* link a large number of conditions together. If this was a Mathematical Proof class, I might have you figure out something like `"Condition_A | Condition_B & (Condition_C & Condition_D) | Condition_E"` where A, B, and E are TRUE while C and D are FALSE.



But this isn't a Proofs class, so we can enjoy ourselves instead, and move onto the `arrange()` function. 

Two shorthands worth knowing before we leave `filter()`, because they save
brackets in exactly the situations that generate bugs:

```{r}
# between(x, lo, hi) is equivalent to (x >= lo) & (x <= hi), inclusive at both ends
filter(food_cpi_mutate, between(Year, 2010, 2012))

# %in% tests membership in a set, and replaces a chain of == joined by |
filter(food_cpi_mutate, Year %in% c(2008, 2009, 2022))
```

Use `between()` for a numeric range and `%in%` for a list of allowed values.
Writing `Year == 2008 | Year == 2009 | Year == 2022` gives the same three rows
and is three times as easy to typo.




### 3.6 a) `arrange()`

`arrange()` is a fairly simple function for reordering a dataset. You feed it a dataframe and one or more columns:

```{r}
arrange(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent)
```

It returns your dataframe, ordered by the specified column. By default, in Ascending order (lowest to greatest).

`NA` sorts to the bottom regardless of direction. `arrange()` is the one verb
that does not drop missing values, it parks them at the end. So 2000 is still
there, at the very bottom of the object, even though its `food_change_percent`
is unknown. Note that the tibble prints only the first 10 of 23 rows and ends
with `# i 13 more rows`, so you will not see 2000 on screen here. Run
`tail(arrange(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent))` to bring it into view.

The smallest actual value is 2017 at 0.07 percent, a year in which the food
index moved from 142.6 to 142.7. The row order changed; nothing else did.
`arrange()` never adds, removes or alters a value.

By wrapping the column in `desc()`, you can get Descending order (greatest to lowest).

```{r}
arrange(food_cpi_mutate, desc(food_change_percent))
```

2022 is on top at 8.89 percent, followed by 2009 at 4.93 and 2001 at 4.39. Those
are the same three years `filter(food_change_percent > 4)` returned in Section
3.5, which is a useful cross-check: sorting and filtering should agree with each
other.

You can also arrange by multiple columns; it prioritizes by column order. So, `arrange(df, col1, col2)` will be arranged first in ascending order of `col1`, but wherever rows have the same `col1` value, ties are broken by `col2`

```{r}
arrange(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent, food_change)
```

With continuous data such as ours, there are very rarely ties to be broken, so arranging by `food_change_percent` and `food_change` works out the same as just arranging by `food_change_percent`.

Second sort keys earn their keep on categorical data. `arrange(df, decade, desc(Food))`,
once `decade` exists in Section 3.8, would list the decades in order and put the
highest-priced year first inside each one. That is a common way to lay out a
results table before exporting it.


### 3.6 b) Ceci n'est pas une pipe

`arrange()` combos nicely with `slice()`. First, arrange a dataframe, then get the top X number of rows by using `slice(df, 1:X)`.

`slice()` selects rows by position, not by value. `1:5` is R's way of writing the
sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, so `slice(df, 1:5)` returns the first five rows of
whatever it is handed. It has no idea what "top" means; the sorting is what makes
the first five rows the top five.

Or better yet, start using `%>%`, also known as "pipes". Pipes are a tool that lets you easily chain multiple steps, passing the output of one function to the next step for further analysis. 

Pipes do not come in basic R, but are imported with the TidyVerse.

The mechanical rule is short: **`x %>% f(y)` is rewritten by R as `f(x, y)`.**
The value on the left is inserted as the *first* argument of the function on the
right. That is exactly why every `dplyr` verb takes a data frame first. The
design of the verbs and the design of the pipe are the same decision.

```{r}
# good syntax

food_cpi_mutate %>%                         # takes food_cpi_mutate and passes it forward:
  arrange(desc(food_change_percent)) %>%    # arranges in descending order by food_change_percent and passes it forward
  slice(1:5)                                # slices to first five results
```

As you see, this starts with a dataframe, then "pipes" it into `arrange(desc(food_change_percent))`, and then pipes that result into `slice(1:5)`

Note that neither `arrange()` nor `slice()` names a data frame anywhere in that
chain. Each one receives it from the pipe. Note also that nothing was assigned,
so `food_cpi_mutate` is unchanged and the five-row result was printed and
discarded. To keep it: `top_5 <- food_cpi_mutate %>% arrange(...) %>% slice(1:5)`.

Compare it with

```{r}
# bad syntax

slice(arrange(food_cpi_mutate, desc(food_change_percent)), 1:5)
```

Both of these get the same result. But our "good" syntax has a much clearer flow to it, almost like a sentence:

"Take `food_cpi_mutate` and arrange it in descending order by `food_change_percent`, and then slice the result from 1 to 5"

Indeed, a major part of why Pipes are useful is that they "read" from top down, left to right. In contrast, wrapping functions reads right-to-left, inside to outside. Imagine pseudocode in either of two cases:

```
dataframe %>%
  function_1(argument_a) %>%
  function_2(argument_b, argument_c) %>%
  function_3(argument_d)
```

Compare this to:

```
function_3(function_2(function_1(dataframe, argument_a), argument_b, argument_c), argument_d)
```

The second statement is *far* more difficult to read, particularly with the function arguments added. 

There is a practical reason beyond readability. To debug the piped version you
delete the last `%>%` line and re-run, and you see the intermediate result. To
debug the nested version you have to count brackets. On a five-step chain, that
difference is the difference between finding a bug in ten seconds and in ten
minutes.

Three details about pipes that come up constantly:

- **Where the `%>%` goes.** It must end the line, not start the next one. R
  reads line by line and treats a line that looks complete as complete, so a
  leading `%>%` produces a syntax error.
- **The native pipe.** Since R 4.1 the language itself has a pipe, written `|>`,
  which needs no package. For plain `x |> f()` calls it behaves the same as
  `%>%`, and this document uses `%>%` throughout because that is what almost all
  existing tidyverse code uses.
- **Placing the value somewhere other than first.** With `%>%` a dot `.` stands
  for the piped value, so `x %>% lm(Food ~ Year, data = .)` works. You will need
  this for any function whose first argument is not the data.

```{r}
# All three lines do the same thing.
nrow(food_cpi_mutate)
food_cpi_mutate %>% nrow()
food_cpi_mutate |> nrow()
```

The top five years are easier to compare as bars than as a table.

```{r}
top_5_food <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  arrange(desc(food_change_percent)) %>%
  slice(1:5)

ggplot(top_5_food,
       aes(x = fct_reorder(factor(Year), food_change_percent),
           y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  # coord_flip() swaps the axes so the year labels read horizontally.
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 0c: Five largest yearly increases in the food CPI",
    x     = "Year",
    y     = "Food CPI change (percent)"
  )
```

2022 is roughly twice the size of the second-largest year, 2009, and the fourth
and fifth bars are almost the same height. A ranked table hides that shape; the
bar chart makes it obvious that "top five" here means one extreme year plus four
ordinary ones.

The x aesthetic in that plot is worth unpacking, because it is the first factor
in this document. `Year` is numeric, and `geom_col()` on a numeric x axis draws
bars at numeric positions and sorts them by year. We want them sorted by size.
`factor(Year)` converts the years to a categorical variable, whose *levels* are
the allowed categories in the order `ggplot2` will draw them; by default that
order is alphabetical. `fct_reorder(f, x)` then reorders the levels of `f` by
the values of `x`, so the levels run from smallest percentage change to largest,
and `coord_flip()` puts the largest at the top.

An alternative to `arrange() %>% slice()` for exactly this job:

```{r}
# slice_max() sorts and slices in one step. n = 5 asks for five rows.
slice_max(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent, n = 5) %>%
  select(Year, food_change_percent)
```

Use `slice_max()` or `slice_min()` when all you want is the top or bottom few
rows; use `arrange()` when the sorted order of the whole table matters, for
instance because you are about to print or export it.


fourth exercise does want `desc()`. The point of pairing them is that "slice the
first ten" means something different depending on how you sorted.




### 3.7 `summarise()`

`summarise()` is used for making bespoke summary statistics.

You can get a generic set of summary statistics by passing your dataframe into the `summary()` function, as shown:

```{r}
summary(food_cpi_mutate)
```

`summary()` is base R and prints one block per column: minimum, first quartile,
median, mean, third quartile, maximum. Two things to read here. In the
`food_change_percent` block the median is 2.45 while the mean is 2.82, so the
mean sits above the middle observation, which is the signature of a right skew
caused by a few large years. And all four lagged columns carry an extra line,
`NA's :1`, reporting the missing 2000 value. `summary()` tells you about missing
data without being asked. Most other functions do not.

However, you'll often want to get more specific stats. `summary()` gives us measures of the values themselves - Min/Max, quantiles, Mean - but nothing related to variance. It's also just raw data over the whole dataset without grouping. 

As we'll see, `summarise()` offers us a lot more control over what statistics we calculate. 

To use `summarise()`, you first feed in a dataframe. Then, you tell it how to make the variables you want, and these are returned as a new dataframe. To illustrate:

```{r}
food_cpi_mutate %>% 
  summarise(mean_Food = mean(Food),
            mean_food_change = mean(food_change),
            sd_Food = sd(Food),
            sd_food_change = sd(food_change))


```

The output is a one-row tibble. That is the defining behavior of `summarise()`
and the thing that separates it from `mutate()`: `mutate()` returns as many rows
as it received, `summarise()` collapses them to one row per group, and with no
grouping the whole table is one group.

The naming works the same way as in `mutate()`. `mean_Food = mean(Food)` says
"make a column called `mean_Food` holding the result of `mean()` applied to the
`Food` column".

(Notice the `NA` values in the `mean_food_change` and `sd_food_change` columns!)

`mean_Food` is 126.69 and `sd_Food` is 21.70, both fine. `mean_food_change` and
`sd_food_change` are `NA`, because one of the 23 values fed into them is `NA`
and `NA` contaminates any arithmetic it touches. R is not broken here; it is
refusing to invent a number for the 2000 change.

There's a whole range of functions you can use here.

There are your more basic, standard statistical measures, some of which turn up in `summary()`:

-   `sum()`: Calculates the sum of values in a column.
-   `min()`: Returns the minimum value in a column.
-   `max()`: Returns the maximum value in a column.
-   `median()`: Calculates the median of values in a column.
-   `sd()`: Computes the standard deviation of values in a column.
-   `var()`: Computes the variance of values in a column.

Then there are the ones more related to the structure and elements of your data:

-   `n()`: Returns the count or number of rows in a group or the entire dataset.
-   `first()`: Returns the first value in a column.
-   `last()`: Returns the last value in a column.
-   `n_distinct()`: Counts the number of distinct or unique values in a column.
-   `quantile()`: Calculates specified quantiles of values in a column.
-   `length()`: Returns the length of a vector or the number of elements in a column.

`n()` is the odd one out: it takes no arguments at all, because it counts rows
rather than reading a column. It only works inside `summarise()`, `mutate()` and
`filter()`, where `dplyr` knows what "the current group" means.

Let's run a bunch of these.

#### NA Note

I mentioned how our `mutate()` function involved taking lags, resulting in our first row having `NA` values in several variables. When we feed these into summary statistic functions, we get problems.

Thankfully, we can tell the functions to ignore these rows, and calculate as though they didn't exist, with the argument `na.rm = TRUE`. We do this for all the functions except `first()` and `last()`; these two are about what's literally in the data column, so it makes sense we don't want to ignore the value!

`na.rm` stands for "NA remove", and it is an argument of the statistical
function, not of `summarise()`. It goes inside the inner brackets:
`mean(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE)`, never
`summarise(..., na.rm = TRUE)`. The default is `FALSE` on purpose. Silently
dropping missing observations changes the sample you are describing, and R makes
you say out loud that you meant to.

```{r}
# Assuming food_cpi_mutate is your dataframe
food_cpi_mutate

food_cpi_mutate %>% 
  summarise(mean_inflation = mean(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_inflation = max(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_inflation = min(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_inflation = sd(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            var_inflation = var(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            first_inflation = first(food_change_percent),
            last_inflation = last(food_change_percent),
            inflation_25 = quantile(food_change_percent, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
            inflation_50 = quantile(food_change_percent, 0.5, na.rm = TRUE),
            inflation_75 = quantile(food_change_percent, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE))

```

Reading the row: mean food inflation over 2001-2022 is 2.82 percent, with a
standard deviation of 1.74. The maximum is 8.89 (2022) and the minimum is 0.07
(2017). Variance is 3.04, which is just the standard deviation squared, so
reporting both is redundant.

`first_inflation` is `NA`. That is the expected answer and the reason the note
above says not to add `na.rm = TRUE` to it: `first()` reports what is literally
in row 1, and row 1 has no value. `last_inflation` is 8.89, the 2022 figure,
because the rows are still in year order. If you had sorted the tibble first,
`first()` and `last()` would report something else entirely. They describe row
position, not time.

The quartiles are worth a second look. The median is 2.45 and the 75th
percentile is 3.46, but the maximum is 8.89. Three quarters of the years sit
under 3.5 percent and one year is nearly triple that. Whenever the gap between
`p75` and the maximum is that large, expect an outlier to dominate any
regression you fit later, which is exactly what Section 4.3 shows.

There won't be an exercise for this section, because we're going to join `summarise()` with a function that adds a lot more power. 



### 3.8 `group_by()`

`group_by()` divides a DataFrame into "groups" based on having shared values in one or more columns. You can then run summary statistics across these to extract information about how they differ.

`group_by()` on its own changes nothing you can see; it attaches a label to the
data frame saying "treat these rows as belonging together". The next verb in the
chain then does its work once per group instead of once for the whole table.
That is the entire idea, and it turns `summarise()` from a one-row report into a
comparison table.

Unfortunately for us, the `Year` changes every year. All our other variables are continuous, making them highly unlikely to share common values. There's also not much meaningful information conveyed by two years both having a `food_change_percent` value of, say, 4.92653414.

So, we'll quickly create some new variables which *do* split the data into groups.

The next chunk builds two grouping columns. It also reassigns `food_cpi_mutate`,
so from this point on that object has 9 columns rather than 7. Every later
chunk, including the plots in Section 4, depends on `decade` existing, so run
this one before skipping ahead.

```{r}
# Create 'even_years' column
food_cpi_mutate <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  mutate(even_years = ifelse(Year %% 2 == 0, 1, 0))

# Create 'decade' column
food_cpi_mutate <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  mutate(decade = case_when(
    Year >= 2000 & Year <= 2009 ~ "00s",
    Year >= 2010 & Year <= 2019 ~ "10s",
    Year >= 2020 ~ "20s",
    TRUE ~ "Unknown"
  ))
```

Three pieces of syntax here.

`%%` is the modulo operator: it returns the remainder after division. `2022 %% 2`
is 0 and `2021 %% 2` is 1, so `Year %% 2 == 0` is a `TRUE`/`FALSE` test for
"even year".

`ifelse(test, yes, no)` is a vectorized if-statement. It runs the test on all 23
rows at once and returns `yes` where the test is `TRUE` and `no` where it is
`FALSE`. Here it returns 1 and 0, so `even_years` ends up numeric rather than
logical. Storing a `TRUE`/`FALSE` as 1/0 is a habit from Stata and it works, but
`Year %% 2 == 0` on its own would have given a genuine logical column.

`case_when()` generalizes `ifelse()` to more than two outcomes. Each line has the
form `condition ~ value`, and the conditions are tested **in order**, with the
first match winning. The final `TRUE ~ "Unknown"` is a catch-all: `TRUE` is
always true, so any row that matched nothing above lands there. In this dataset
nothing does, since the years run 2000 to 2022, but writing the fallback is good
practice. Without it, unmatched rows would silently become `NA`.

```{r}
food_cpi_mutate

```

The two new columns are at the right-hand end. `decade` is `<chr>`, a character
column, not a factor. `ggplot2` will sort character values alphabetically, which
for "00s", "10s", "20s" happens to be the correct chronological order. That is
luck, not design: had the labels been "2000s" and "90s", alphabetical order
would have put the 1990s last.

Now we can see if our stats varied systematically between even and odd years, and by decade.

```{r}

# Calculate summary statistics ignoring NA values
food_cpi_mutate %>%
  group_by(even_years) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_Food = mean(Food),
    avg_food_change = mean(food_change, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_food_change_percent = mean(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE)
)


```

Two rows out, one per value of `even_years`, and the grouping column is carried
into the output automatically so you can tell which row is which. Odd years
(`even_years = 0`) average 2.796 percent food inflation and even years average
2.843 percent. A gap of five hundredths of a percentage point across 22
observations is noise. That is the useful result: the calendar's parity does not
predict inflation, and now you have shown it rather than assumed it.

Note that `avg_Food` did not need `na.rm = TRUE` because the `Food` column has
no missing values, while the two lagged columns did. Add the argument where the
data requires it, not everywhere out of habit.

One behavior to know about: after `group_by()` and `summarise()`, the result may
still carry grouping information if you grouped by more than one column, and a
message will say so. `summarise(..., .groups = "drop")` returns a plain
ungrouped tibble and silences the message. `ungroup()` at the end of a chain
does the same job.

Grouped means are easier to compare as bars.

```{r}
decade_means <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  group_by(decade) %>%
  summarise(
    n_years                 = n(),   # rows in this group
    avg_food_change_percent = mean(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

decade_means

ggplot(decade_means, aes(x = decade, y = avg_food_change_percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  # geom_text() writes the value on top of each bar. vjust = -0.4 nudges the
  # label just above the bar rather than inside it.
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_food_change_percent, 2)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 0d: Average yearly food CPI change, by decade",
    x     = "Decade",
    y     = "Mean food CPI change (percent)"
  )
```

The 2010s averaged 2.16 percent, the 2000s 2.97 percent, and the three years of
the 2020s in this sample 4.56 percent. Read the `n_years` column before reading
the bars: the 00s and 10s each contain 10 years, the 20s only 3. A mean of three
observations, one of which is the 2022 outlier, is not comparable evidence to a
mean of ten. Reporting the group size next to the group mean is not optional
politeness; it is what stops the reader from over-reading the third bar.
