## 4. Introduction to Data Visualization: `ggplot2`


### 4.1 Basics of `ggplot2`

1. Background

`ggplot2` follows the "grammar of graphics" approach to data visualization, breaking graphs down into their separate fundamental parts. These components - your geometric objects, aesthetic mappings, scales, etc - are added or modified *individually* and directly with `ggplot2` functions.

This creates a sequential process to building visualizations, where sophisticated plots can be created with simple components. 

The practical consequence is that you build a plot by addition. Every `ggplot2`
plot is a `ggplot()` call plus one or more layers, joined with `+`:

```
ggplot(data = DATA, mapping = aes(MAPPINGS)) +
  geom_FUNCTION() +
  labs(TITLES AND AXIS NAMES)
```

Two syntax points before anything else.

The connector is `+`, not `%>%`. This trips up everybody at least once.
`ggplot2` predates the pipe, and its `+` composes plot layers rather than
passing data forward. You can pipe *into* a `ggplot()` call
(`data %>% ggplot(aes(...)) + geom_point()`), but inside the plot it is `+` all
the way down.

Like the pipe, the `+` must end the line. A `+` at the start of a line is a
syntax error, and a *missing* `+` is worse, because R will happily run the first
part as a complete plot and then evaluate the orphaned `geom_` call on its own,
producing an error that names the geom rather than the missing operator.

2. Components of `ggplot2`

- `ggplot()`

This is the function you call to initialize a plot in your R code chunk. You feed in a dataframe or tibble as your `data` argument, upon which your plot will be based. 

On its own, `ggplot(data = df)` draws an empty grey panel. It has data but no
instruction about what to draw or where. Both of those come from the layers.

- Geometric Objects: `geoms`

These are what you're likely most familiar with in data visualization: the lines, bars, points, etc, which actually display your data in visual format. In `ggplot2`, these are all referred to as `geom_` first. Some examples are:

-- `geom_line()`: line plot

-- `geom_point()`: scatter plot

-- `geom_bar()`: bar plot

-- `geom_smooth()`: best fit regression line plot

Geometric objects are added on after your `ggplot()` call after a `+` sign. These can be layered on top of one another to get more intricate plots. If you're plotting a relationship between an `x` and a `Y` variable, you could call both `geom_point()` to show all data points, and then a `geom_smooth()` to show their best-fit linear relationship.

Some geoms function as direct mappings of a data point's value into a visual field. For example, `geom_point()` and `geom_line()` use these values as coordinates on the X and Y axes. Other geoms run some sort of statistical transformation or calculation and display an object based off of this result. `geom_smooth()` is an example of this case, where the best-fit line between your X and Y variables is calculated, and then drawn over your dataset.

Two more geoms used below that draw nothing from the data at all:
`geom_hline(yintercept = 0)` draws a horizontal reference line at a value you
choose, and `geom_vline(xintercept = 2020)` draws a vertical one. They take a
number rather than a column, because they are annotations, not data.

Layer order is drawing order. A `geom_smooth()` written after `geom_point()`
draws its band on top of the points; written before, the points sit on top of
the band. When two layers overlap, the last one wins.

- Aesthetic Mapping: `aes()`

"Aesthetic Mapping" refers to the "mapping", or relation of variables in the data to visual properties (i.e. Aesthetics) in the graph, such as position, colors, shapes, size, etc. They are defined through the `aes()` function, which can be assigned globally (to the whole plot) if passed into the initializing `ggplot()` function, or individually by passing this into the `geom_` functions. 

To map an aesthetic to a variable, assign the aesthetic (several are listed below) as equal to the variable inside your `aes()` statement. R will assign Levels (i.e. distinct values of the shape/size/color) to your data points based on their values in the given variable. Some of the core visual effects you can alter with `aes()` arguments are:

- `shape` (to change the appearance of scatter plot points)

- `size` (setting the size of your visual objects)

- `color` and `fill` (altering color of the outline and interior of objects respectively)

All of these work with discrete variables; `size` and `color` are also compatible with continuous variables. 

For example, consider a grocery store's sales data, which has data on `item_category`, `price`, and `date`. We might build a `geom_point()` plot, with `date` on the x-axis, `price` on the y-axis, and an `aes()` statement with `shape`, `size`, or `color` equal to `item_category` to also describe item types.

Some aesthetics can be set manually. In your `geom_X()` function, but outside of the `aes()` statement, you might pass `color = "blue"`, to make a line or scatter points a specific color.

That last paragraph states the single most important distinction in `ggplot2`,
so it is worth putting a name to it:

- **Mapping** means *inside* `aes()`: `aes(color = decade)` says "let the value
  of `decade` decide the color", so `ggplot2` picks colors, builds a scale, and
  draws a legend.
- **Setting** means *outside* `aes()`: `geom_point(color = "blue")` says "make
  every point blue", full stop. No scale, no legend.

Put a constant inside `aes()` and you get the wrong thing but not an error:
`aes(color = "blue")` creates an invisible one-level variable whose single value
is the text `"blue"`, and `ggplot2` assigns it its first default color, which is
red. Figures 3 and 4 below use that behavior deliberately, with
`scale_color_manual()` to fix the colors afterwards, which is a legitimate trick
for hand-labeling series.

We'll see examples of all of these below!


### 4.2 Line Charts

The first plot maps `Year` to x and `Food` to y, and draws one `geom_line()`.
Note the `mapping = ` argument name: it is optional, because `mapping` is the
second argument of `ggplot()`, but writing it makes the call easier to read.
`labs()` sets the axis names and the title, and every plot you hand in should
have all three.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, mapping = aes(x = Year, y = Food)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Food Price CPI", title = "Fig. 1: Changes in Food Prices over Time")
```

The food index climbs from 93.3 in 2000 to 171.5 in 2022, and the line is close
to straight for the whole period except the final segment, which is much
steeper. Nothing else in the plot competes for attention, which is what a
single-series line chart is for.

This is a fairly basic, serviceable line chart. Everybody gets what it means; no professor will fail you over it. But we can do more with it, customizing color and adding more lines to show a broad range of data.

```{r}
ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, mapping = aes(x = Year, y = Food)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se=FALSE) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Food Price CPI", title = "Fig 2: Scatter+Regplot of Food Prices over Time")
```

Two layers share the one `aes()` from the `ggplot()` call: the points and the
fitted line both use `Year` and `Food`. `method = "lm"` fits an ordinary least
squares regression of `Food` on `Year`, and `se = FALSE` turns off the grey
confidence band that `geom_smooth()` draws by default. The message R prints,
`geom_smooth() using formula = 'y ~ x'`, is telling you the model it fitted; it
is a message, not a warning, and it appears every time unless you name the
formula yourself.

The fitted line has a slope of about 3.18 index points per year and an R-squared
of 0.985, so a straight line in calendar time explains almost all of the
variation. Instead of a lineplot, this visualization shows the individual data points with a `geom_point` object, and a linear best fit line with `geom_smooth`. It very starkly shows how food prices jump far off their long-run trend in the final time period, as COVID-era high inflation kicks in. 

Quantify that last point rather than eyeballing it: the regression predicts a
2022 food index of 161.6, and the actual value is 171.5. The final point sits
about 10 index points above trend, which is the largest gap anywhere in the
sample.




```{r}
ggplot(data = food_cpi_mutate) +
  geom_line(aes(x = Year, y = All_items_but_food_energy, color = "All_items_but_food_energy")) +
  geom_line(aes(x = Year, y = Food, color = "Food")) +
  labs(title = "Fig. 3: CPI Price Comparisons Over Time",
       x = "Year", y = "Price") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "red"),
                     labels = c("All-items", "Food"),
                     name = "Data Series:")
```

This plot uses the constant-inside-`aes()` trick described in Section 4.1. Each
`geom_line()` gets its own `aes()`, with its own `y` column and a `color` set to
a quoted label. `ggplot2` treats those two labels as the two levels of an
invisible categorical variable, and builds a legend from them.
`scale_color_manual()` then takes control of that scale: `values` assigns the
colors, `labels` rewrites the text shown in the legend, and `name` titles the
legend.

The order matters and is easy to get wrong. `values` and `labels` are matched to
the *levels*, which are sorted alphabetically, not to the order the
`geom_line()` calls appear. Here `"All_items_but_food_energy"` sorts before
`"Food"`, so `"blue"` goes to the all-items series and `"red"` to food. Swap the
two `geom_line()` lines and the colors do not move; change one of the quoted
labels to something starting with "Z" and they do.

`All-items` falls behind `Food` starting roughly in 2005, gradually diverging until roughly 2021. Both tick up with much higher inflation than before, but `Food` does so much more sharply. 

Repeating a `geom_line()` per series works, but it does not scale: five series
means five near-identical layers and five chances to typo a column name. The
tidyverse answer is to reshape the data into long form first, then draw one
layer.

```{r}
# pivot_longer() turns the two value columns into two rows per year: one column
# says which series the value came from, another holds the value itself.
cpi_long <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  select(Year, Food, All_items_but_food_energy) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(Food, All_items_but_food_energy),
    names_to  = "series",
    values_to = "index_value"
  )

# 46 rows now instead of 23: two series times 23 years.
head(cpi_long, 4)

ggplot(cpi_long, aes(x = Year, y = index_value, color = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  # Naming the values explicitly removes the alphabetical-order trap above.
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("All_items_but_food_energy" = "blue", "Food" = "red"),
    labels = c("All_items_but_food_energy" = "All-items excl. food and energy",
               "Food" = "Food"),
    name   = "Data Series:"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 3b: Fig. 3 redrawn from long-format data",
    x     = "Year",
    y     = "CPI (2002 = 100)"
  )
```

The picture is identical to Figure 3, which is the point: same data, one
`geom_line()` instead of two, and `color = series` is now a genuine mapping to a
real column rather than a trick with quoted constants. Naming the values as
`"column_value" = "color"` pairs also makes the assignment explicit, so
alphabetical ordering stops mattering. Use the repeated-`geom_line()` form for
two series when you are in a hurry, and `pivot_longer()` for anything larger or
anything you will have to edit again.

Let's take a look at their percentage growths over time. 

```{r}
ggplot(data = food_cpi_mutate) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(x = Year, y = All_items_change_percent, color = "All_items")) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(x = Year, y = food_change_percent, color = "Food")) +
  labs(title = "Fig. 4: CPI Percentage Changes Over Time",
       x = "Year", y = "Yearly change (percent)") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "red"),
                     labels = c("All_items", "Food"),
                     name = "Data Series:")
```

Same construction as Figure 3, different columns. Both lines start in 2001
rather than 2000, because the 2000 values are `NA` and `geom_line()` cannot draw
a segment to a missing point.

So, `Food` has consistently higher percentage changes over most of the 2004+ period. How big are these? 

The red line sits above the blue one in 17 of the 22 years. The exceptions are
2002, 2003, 2016, 2017 and 2018. Notice also how much flatter the blue line is:
the all-items series stays between 0.86 and 4.96 percent, while food ranges from
0.07 to 8.89.

We can actually pass in a modified value as the `y` value in our `geom_line` function. If we subtract `All_items_change_percent` from `food_change_percent`, we get the difference in these values (amazing!) which can be plotted directly. Positive values show when food prices are growing faster; negative values show when All Items are growing faster.

Doing arithmetic inside `aes()` is worth noticing on its own. `ggplot2` evaluates
the expression against the data frame, so any calculation you could put in
`mutate()` can go straight into the mapping. Do it for a quick look; do it in
`mutate()` when the derived variable is part of the analysis, so it is stored,
inspectable and reusable.

```{r}

ggplot(data = food_cpi_mutate) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(x = Year, y = food_change_percent - All_items_change_percent), color = "turquoise") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Fig 5. Difference in CPI Percentage Change Over Time",
       x = "Year", y = "Percentage Growth Difference") +
  scale_color_manual(values = "turquoise")
```

Here `color = "turquoise"` sits *outside* `aes()`, so it is a setting, not a
mapping: the line is turquoise and there is no legend. The
`scale_color_manual()` call on the last line therefore does nothing at all,
because no color aesthetic was mapped for it to control. It is harmless, and it
is a good illustration of the mapping-versus-setting distinction: a scale
function can only modify a scale that exists.

The dashed `geom_hline()` at zero is doing real work. On a difference plot the
zero line is the whole reference frame, and without it the reader has to hunt
along the y axis to see which side of nothing a point is on.

The differences in their growth rates (Food minus All items) is also consistently positive, meaning Food inflation consistently outpaces normal inflation.

Read the line against the dashed zero before accepting that. The difference is
positive in 17 of the 22 years and negative in five: 2002, 2003, 2016, 2017 and
2018. "Usually positive, and positive in every year since 2019" is what the data
supports. The peak is 2022, where food inflation exceeds all-items inflation by
3.93 percentage points.

You could say that `Fig. 4` and `Fig. 5` are two ways of showing the same data; `5` is a transformation of the data in `4`. This reduces the information conveyed by `Fig. 5`; in a year with an inflation of difference of 2%, we could have Food/All-items inflations of 4% and 2%, or of 100% and 98%!

Does this make `Fig. 5` a worse plot than `Fig. 4`? Not necessarily. **It all comes down to what you are trying to visualize.** If the important relation is the difference itself, then `Fig. 5` is the way to go. By reducing the information it shows, it focuses attention onto what matters most. 




#### Exercises (`geom_line()`)


1. Visualize `"Food"` and `"All_items_but_food_energy"` on the Y axis and `"Year"` on the x-axis. Include a vertical line to show when the COVID period begins.

You can make a vertical line with the `geom_vline()` function. You specify where it goes with the `xintercept` argument; make this equal to whatever year is appropriate. 

```{r}
colnames(food_cpi_mutate)

```

```{r}

ggplot(data = food_cpi_mutate) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(
    x = Year, y = All_items_but_food_energy,
    color = "All_items_but_food_energy"
  )) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(x = Year, y = Food, color = "Food")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2020) +
  labs(
    title = "Exercise 1: CPI with Vline",
    x = "Year", y = "CPI"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("blue", "red"),
    labels = c("All-items", "Food"),
    name = "Data Series:"
  )


```

The vertical line is at 2020 because that is when the pandemic starts, but the
break in the series is not there. Both lines carry on at their old slopes
through 2020. The all-items line bends upward in 2021 and again in 2022. Food
does not bend until 2022: its 2021 increase of 3.8 is smaller than its 2015 and
2019 increases of 5.0 and 4.9, whereas its 2022 increase is 14.0. The figure is a good example
of an annotation that is defensible but does not mark what the reader assumes it
marks, so say in the caption whether the line is an event date or an estimated
break.

For a dashed line instead of solid, add `linetype = "dashed"` as in Figure 5.
Both arguments sit outside `aes()`, because they are settings.

2. Use `durables_cpi` to visualize the CPI of the different product types over time. 

Five series, so this is the case where `pivot_longer()` pays off. The shape to
aim for is one row per year per product type, then a single `geom_line()` with
`color` mapped to the product-type column. `durables_cpi` gained an
`avg_durables_cpi` column in Exercise 3 below if you run that chunk first, so
select the columns you want rather than piping the whole tibble in.

```{r}


```


3. Take `services_cpi` and `durables_cpi`. For each, calculate an average of their CPI values using `mutate()`, or any other method of your choice. Create `averaged_cpi` by using the `bind_cols()` function to retrieve these from their respective Tibbles, along with the `Year` variable from one. Then plot the two series in a line plot, called `"Exercise 3: Durable VS Service CPI"`

**This one is hard. Multiple steps and will require some guidance.**
```{r}
colnames(durables_cpi)
colnames(services_cpi)
```

The plan below is: add an average column to each tibble, keep only what you need
from each, glue them side by side, then plot. `bind_cols()` joins two data frames
column-wise by *position*, so it assumes both are sorted identically and have the
same number of rows. That is true here because both came from `cpi_t` in the same
row order. It would not be true in general, and the safer tool for real work is
a join such as `left_join(x, y, by = "Year")`, which matches on a key instead of
trusting the row order.

```{r}
#colnames(durables_cpi)
#colnames(services_cpi)


# Calculate `avg_durable_cpi`

durables_cpi <- durables_cpi %>% mutate(
  avg_durables_cpi= (Household_operations_furniture_equipment+Clothing_and_footwear+Shelter+Transportation+Recreation_education_books) / 5
)

durables_cpi
#avg using all durables data


# Select `Year` and `avg_durable_cpi` as new dataframe in preparation for `bind_cols` later

durables_cpi_select <- durables_cpi %>% select(
  Year, avg_durables_cpi
)

durables_cpi_select

# Calculate `avg_service_cpi` just as with durables case

#same as the avg_durable_cpi calcualtion
services_cpi<- services_cpi %>% mutate(
  avg_services_cpi = (Health_personal_care + Services) / 2
)

services_cpi


# Select `avg_service_cpi` in prep for `bind_cols`

services_cpi_select <- services_cpi %>% select(
  avg_services_cpi
)


# make `averaged_cpi` tibble for plotting

averaged_cpi <- bind_cols(durables_cpi_select, services_cpi_select)
averaged_cpi

# plotting averaged cpi values


```

`averaged_cpi` ends up with three columns: `Year`, `avg_durables_cpi` and
`avg_services_cpi`. Only `durables_cpi_select` kept `Year`, which is why
`bind_cols()` does not produce a duplicate. Had both kept it, `bind_cols()`
would have renamed the second copy `Year...3` rather than failing, which is the
kind of silent mess that makes joins the better habit.

Two things to think about before you plot. This average weights each component
equally, whereas Statistics Canada weights them by expenditure share, so
`avg_durables_cpi` is not an official aggregate and should not be described as
one. And the five durable components are on the same 2002 = 100 base, so
averaging them is at least dimensionally sensible; averaging a price index with,
say, a dollar value would not be.


### 4.3 Scatter Plots


Another fundamental type of plot is the Scatter Plot, where we establish X and Y axes and represent data points as dots in their respective locations. This allows us to visualize the distribution of our data along chosen dimensions, and can be extended in `ggplot2`, with other variables denoted through the size or shape of our scatter points.

You might actually consider a line chart to be a specialized form of a scatter plot, with the points represented and then consecutive points represented with straight lines. `Fig. 2` also shows the similar option of adding a linear best-fit line to show the overall statistical relationship, rather than the standard line plot approach. We'll try this too.

One change from Section 4.2 that is easy to miss: from here on, time is no
longer on the x axis. The plots below put one percentage change against another,
so each point is a year but the years are not in order along the axis. A scatter
plot answers "how do these two variables move together", not "what happened
when".

```{r}
ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 6: Scatterplot of Food vs Non-Food CPI Changes")
```

R prints a warning here: one row was removed because it contains a missing
value. That is 2000, whose lagged columns are `NA`. The warning is correct
behavior and worth leaving visible rather than silencing, because a plot quietly
dropping rows is exactly the sort of thing you want to be told about.

About as simply as possible, we get a look at how data points are distributed along the `Food` and `All items but food and energy` CPI types. Outliers are not statistically identified, but we do get some idea from visual inspection; a clumping around "normal" inflation levels, with one extreme value at over twice the average inflation value. 

Excluding the outlier, the points span 0.86 to 2.77 percent on the x axis and
0.07 to 4.93 percent on the y axis, with most of them packed into the lower left.
The lone point at (4.96, 8.89) is 2022, more than three times the mean food
inflation of 2.82 percent. Remember which year it is; the rest of this section is
largely about what that one point does to a fitted line.

```{r}
ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent, shape = decade)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 7a. Previous with Decade shown via Shape")

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent, size = decade)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 7b. Previous with Decade shown via Size")


ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent, color = decade)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 7c. Previous with Decade shown via Color")
```

The `aes()` function called in our initializing `ggplot()` function lets us set features for the whole plot. These `aesthetics` can be very useful for conveying more information without using new space, a third dimension, or other complicated features. In `Figs 7a-c`, we see three different ways, using `shape`, `size`, and `color`.

All three plots contain identical data, mapped to `decade` three different ways.
Note that Figure 7b prints an extra warning that the other two do not:
"Using size for a discrete variable is not advised." `ggplot2` is telling you
that `size` is an *ordered, quantitative* channel. A bigger dot reads as "more
of something", and the reader will try to interpret the ordering. That is fine
when the variable really is ordered, as decades happen to be, and misleading for
an unordered category like province or product type.

Which of these is the best?

Shape?

Size? 

Color?

Judge them on three criteria rather than taste. How many levels can the channel
carry before it becomes unreadable? Does the channel imply an order that the
variable does not have? And will it survive greyscale printing and the roughly
8 percent of men with red-green color vision deficiency? Apply those to the three
figures above and to a hypothetical version with twelve categories instead of
three, and the answer usually stops being a matter of opinion.

```{r}
ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, mapping = aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 8a. Food, All-items CPI with Linear Best-Fit Line")
```


This is the same fundamental relationship as before, but now visualized with a best fit line, provided by `geom_smooth()`. This "best fit" is decided by our familiar linear regression method because we specified `method = "lm"`. Other options are available. `geom_smooth()` defaults to `"auto"`, which uses an internal selection method:

The grey band around the line is the 95 percent confidence interval for the
conditional mean, drawn because `se` defaults to `TRUE` here; Figure 2 turned it
off with `se = FALSE`. Where the band is wide, the fitted line is poorly pinned
down. It flares out at the right-hand end, which is the plot telling you that
the slope is being carried by a single point out there.

The fitted slope is 1.32: a one point rise in all-items inflation comes with a
1.32 point rise in food inflation, and the R-squared is 0.41. Drop 2022 and refit
and the slope falls to 0.004 with an R-squared of 0.000004. One observation out
of 22 accounts for the entire relationship. That is not a reason to delete the
point; it is a reason to report both numbers.

```{r}
ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, mapping = aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "auto") + 
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 8b. Food, All-items CPI with Local Regression Best-Fit Line")
```

It defaults to `"loess"`, or local regression, a more flexible technique that involves multiple polynomials. 

The message R prints confirms it: `geom_smooth() using method = 'loess' and
formula = 'y ~ x'`. The rule `geom_smooth()` applies is size-based, using loess
for fewer than 1000 observations and a generalized additive model above that. So
`"auto"` on a small sample and `"auto"` on a large one fit different models, and
a plot whose method changes when you add data is not a plot you want in a paper.
Name the method.

Between Figures `8a` and `8b`, both are clearly imperfect. Our outlier almost certainly has heavy leverage on the final result. In normal circumstances, defaulting to `"lm"` is safe and easily explainable, being the direct correlation between your variables rather than a "black box" model decided by R, and so `"lm"` would be my general recommendation. 

The refit above makes "heavy leverage" precise rather than impressionistic. Loess
is affected differently: it fits locally, so 2022 bends only the right-hand end
of the curve instead of tilting the whole line, which is why the middle of the
loess curve is nearly flat while the OLS line slopes.

When one point matters this much, label it. The chunk below draws the same
scatter and writes the year next to any point above 4 percent food inflation.

```{r}
ggplot(food_cpi_mutate,
       aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  # A geom can take its own data argument. Here only the high-inflation rows are
  # passed to geom_text(), so only those three points get labeled.
  geom_text(
    data    = filter(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent > 4),
    mapping = aes(label = Year),
    nudge_y = 0.35,   # move the label up a little so it clears the point
    size    = 3
  ) +
  # formula = y ~ x states the model explicitly and silences the message.
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Fig 8c. Fig 8a with the high-inflation years labeled",
    x     = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
    y     = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)"
  )
```

The three labeled points are 2022, 2009 and 2001, the same three `filter()`
returned in Section 3.5. 2022 sits far up and to the right of everything else,
while 2009 and 2001 are high on the y axis but ordinary on the x axis: those were
years of high food inflation without high general inflation. 2022 is the only
year where both moved together, which is why it alone controls the slope.

Passing `data =` to a single geom is the general mechanism worth taking away.
Layers inherit the plot's data and mappings by default, and either can be
overridden per layer. That is how you annotate a subset, overlay a second data
source, or highlight specific observations.

4. Make a scatterplot with `Year` on the x-axis, `Food` on the Y-axis, and a linear trendline. Make sure to give it an appropriate `title` in the `labs()` argument!

```{r}


```

As we can see, we have a fairly strong fit of our data points to our linear best-fit line; inflation increases prices by a roughly equal amount between most periods. 

The regression behind that plot has an R-squared of 0.985 and a slope of 3.18
index points per year, so "fairly strong" is an understatement for the fit and
"roughly equal amount" is the right reading of the slope: the index gains about
the same number of points each year, not the same percentage.

Note that with inflation being targeted to 2%, this would suggest over longer periods any linear relation in CPI would break down, as the compounding increases cause bigger and bigger gaps. However, this is not a problem on our ~20 year timeline. 

The mechanism is worth stating plainly. Constant *percentage* growth is
exponential in levels, so a genuinely constant 2 percent inflation would curve
upward on this plot, not run straight. Over 23 years at 2 percent the curvature
is too small to see against the year-to-year noise. Over 60 years it would
dominate, and the linear fit would be visibly wrong.



5. Make a scatter plot with `food_change_percent` on the Y-axis, Year on the x-axis, and a `geom_smooth()`. For the best fit line, try both `"lm"` and `"loess"` and pick whichever you feel works best.

```{r}

```

Now, plotting our percentage increases directly, we see that their trajectory is largely flat. They're mostly distributed around a constant average near 2.8% with random dispersions. As we've seen many times, 2022 is a major outlier, and by a proportionally greater amount than in the `Exercise 4` plot of price levels.

Numbers for that claim: the mean is 2.82 percent, and regressing
`food_change_percent` on `Year` gives a slope of 0.036 percentage points per
year with an R-squared of 0.018 and a p-value of 0.56. Flat, and not
distinguishable from flat.



6. An interesting point of discussion is how these results fit together. The `Exercise 4` plot shows us a roughly constant increase in CPI level; the `Exercise 5` plot shows inflation varies year to year, but has no long-run trend in any particular direction. **Do these results make sense together? Discuss with your partners, then as a group.**

Two things to have straight before you argue about it. A price index and its
growth rate are different objects: one is a level, the other is a first
difference expressed as a share of the previous level. And "no trend in the
growth rate" is a statement about the *second* derivative of the level series,
not the first. Work out what a perfectly constant 2.8 percent inflation rate
would produce in the Exercise 4 plot, and what a perfectly constant 3.18
index-points-per-year increase would produce in the Exercise 5 plot, and the
question mostly answers itself.







# Conclusion

During Workshop 1, we went over the basics of R programming, and the methods you should always try to keep in mind, regardless of what you're doing. Today, we focused on specifics.

In Section 3, we introduced `dplyr`, a very powerful tool for data cleaning. No matter the project, the data you get will never be fully ready to start running your model. There will always be issues with it, cleaning and transformations that need to be carried out. `dplyr` gives us many different tools, reaching well beyond the methods I taught today, and I expect you'll use most of these on any serious empirical project.

In Section 4, we focused on data visualization using `ggplot2`. Part of the same `tidyverse` library as `dplyr`, it allows us to assemble sophisticated and custom-built plots from simple components. This will be useful both in the initial exploration of your data when starting a project, and when displaying your final results. 

## What to take away

The six `dplyr` verbs, and the one sentence that describes each:

| Verb | What it changes |
|------|-----------------|
| `select()` | which columns you keep, and their order |
| `mutate()` | adds columns computed from existing ones |
| `filter()` | which rows you keep, based on a logical test |
| `arrange()` | the order of the rows |
| `summarise()` | collapses many rows into one row of statistics |
| `group_by()` | makes the verb after it run once per group |

All six take a data frame first, return a new data frame, and never modify the
original. That is what makes `%>%` work, and it is why an unassigned result is
printed and lost.

For `ggplot2`, the skeleton is always data, then mappings inside `aes()`, then
one or more `geom_` layers joined with `+`, then `labs()`. The distinction that
causes the most confusion is mapping (inside `aes()`, driven by a column,
produces a legend) versus setting (outside `aes()`, a fixed value, no legend).

Three habits from today that generalize past this dataset:

1. Look at the data after every restructuring step. The import chunk in Section
   3.2 has eight of them, and a single wrong one produces a table that looks
   plausible and is wrong.
2. Handle `NA` explicitly. The lagged columns carry one, and it changed the
   behavior of `mean()`, `filter()`, `geom_line()` and `geom_point()` in four
   different ways in this document.
3. Put a number on what a plot appears to show. "Food inflation outpaces general
   inflation" became "in 17 of 22 years, peaking at a 3.93 point gap in 2022",
   and "the outlier has leverage" became "the slope falls from 1.32 to 0.004
   without it". The plot finds the claim; the arithmetic settles it.
